confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Iorio, David Edy. 2015. Subject and object marking in Bembe. PhD thesis, Newcastle University. ix+376 pp. Open access:http://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/handle/10443/2791
catalog_locator: sec. 2.1.1 'Vowels', p.22 (p.32: vowel length / no penultimate lengthening); p.23 'Tones' (p.33: tone inventory and H/L minimal pairs); ch.4 p.277 (p.287: 'stress is not a feature in Bantu'); p.206 (p.216: obligatory intonation break).
catalog_quote: [p.22] There is no contrast between long and short vowels in Bembe. Moreover, unlike other Bantu languages, such as Zulu or Chicheŵa, it seems that Bembe does not have any form of automatic lengthening, such as penultimate lengthening, either. [p.23] Tones. Bembe, like the majority of Bantu languages, is a tone language. It presents an inventory of four tones: two simple tones, a high (´) and a low one (`), and two complex tones, a rising (ˇ) and a falling one (ˆ). I do not have enough data that could determine whether the latter two complex tones are independent basic tones or combinations of high and low tones. ... (30) a. ichíka 'to burn' vs. ichika 'to bite'; ikónda 'to thinnen' vs. ikònda 'to marry'; ilónda 'to be difficult' vs. ilònda 'to search' ... b. óó 'chicken' vs. òò 'grandmother' [p.277] According to C&S, the main difference between weak pronouns and clitics is that weak pronouns can bear stress while clitics cannot. This is of no use to us, as stress is not a feature in Bantu.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bembe (Itombwe variety) is described as a tone language with contrastive H vs L (plus rising/falling); no vowel-length contrast and no penultimate lengthening; the author treats stress as absent ('not a feature in Bantu') and gives no word-stress/accent placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal alternations noted: verb-final syllable raised to H in relative clauses and clefts (pp. ~150-160); polar questions by rising intonation (p.166).
new_statements.domain_note: The 'no stress' remark (p.277) is a generic aside about Bantu made in a syntax argument, not a phonological analysis of Bembe prominence; the phonetics section (2.1) itself simply has no stress/accent subsection. Description is of the Itombwe (Fizi territory, South Kivu) variety; author notes other works (Mutombo Huta 1973, Mulengwa 2010, Asende 1996) describe phonetically/phonologically different Bembe varieties (pp.7-8).
new_statements.identity_note: Iorio 2015 describes the Bembe (D54, ISO bmb, bemb1255) variety of Itombwe, Fizi territory, South Kivu, DRC, from diaspora speakers in London/Belgium; he states that earlier works (Mutombo Huta 1973, Mulengwa 2010, Asende 1996) describe phonetically and phonologically different Bembe varieties. Not to be confused with Beembe/Kibeembe H11 of Congo-Brazzaville (beem1239) or Bemba M42 (bemb1257).

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 'Phonetics' (pp.20-26): no vowel-length contrast and, unlike Zulu/Chichewa, apparently no automatic (penultimate) lengthening (p.22); 'Bembe.. is a tone language' with H, L, rising, falling and H/L minimal pairs (p.23). No positive word-stress rule anywhere; p.277 remarks in passing that 'stress is not a feature in Bantu'. Polar questions marked by rising intonation (p.166).
